title: Newsom Signs Sweeping California Election Package to Shield Voting Rights Against Interference
snippet: California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed a slate of legislative safeguards aimed at preventing election interference, criminalizing ballot seizures by law enforcement, and clamping down on undisclosed paid political influencers.
content:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Moving to fortify the state's election apparatus ahead of November, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a comprehensive package of election safeguards Saturday, framing the measures as a critical defense against federal overreach and political interference.

Speaking from the Japanese American National Museum in Los Angeles' Little Tokyo, Newsom explicitly targeted former President Donald Trump's administration and allied local law enforcement officials, warning of mounting threats to democratic norms.

"Donald Trump won’t stop until he can exert dictatorial control over your free vote and disenfranchise millions of people this November," Newsom declared in a statement. "California will stop him at every opportunity. We have no bigger task than fighting to protect the right to vote from interference and meddling — the future of democracy is on the line."

Targeting Unlawful Ballot Seizures and Police Interference

The legislative slate directly addresses recent controversies inside the state, including an incident earlier this year when Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco seized more than 650,000 ballots from a local elections office over unsubstantiated fraud claims. That matter remains under review by the California Supreme Court.

Under Assembly Bill 282, authored by former county election chief and state Assemblymember Gail Pellerin, ordering or carrying out the unlawful seizure of ballots, voting machines, or election records is now a felony punishable by up to four years in prison. A companion measure, Senate Bill 259, makes it a crime to tamper with mail-in ballots during transit.

Another major bill taking effect immediately, Senate Bill 884 by state Sen. Tom Umberg, requires counties to open ballot drop-off locations 30 days before Election Day. It also empowers counties to ban electioneering within 200 feet of polling locations and prohibits police officers from making arrests near voting sites unless responding to crimes against individuals, property damage, or active disruptions to voting.

Increasing Campaign Transparency and Voter Access

Beyond physical election security, the new laws address digital campaign tactics and voting access. Assembly Bill 1664 mandates that local election officials instantly notify the state Attorney General and Secretary of State if law enforcement issues warrants, subpoenas, or launches probes involving election records or hardware.

Newsom also signed measures strengthening the California Voting Rights Act through explicit bans on voter suppression tactics and expanded access to multi-language election materials.

Addressing online electioneering, Assembly Bill 1130 mandates strict transparency rules for political campaigns hiring social media influencers. The law follows controversy during the state's primary election, where political campaigns paid influencers thousands of dollars for promotional videos without clearly disclosing financial ties to voters.

"No one should doubt the degree of our resolve in protecting our democracy," California Secretary of State Shirley Weber said in support of the package. "This legislative package ensures that California voters will not be silenced or intimidated."
